# Block 5: Generalising functions with tidy evaluation {.unnumbered}


```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
```


*Roughly 50 minutes. First why a column name stops working once you pass it into
your own function, and the four patterns that fix it; then those patterns applied
to the running example, so that `make_scatter_plot()` and `fit_model()` work for
any pair of columns.*

Block 4 left one limitation. One pipeline now fits a model per group, whatever the
group is, but `fit_model()` still fits only body mass on flipper length, and
`make_scatter_plot()` from Block 3 still plots only those two columns. The fix is
to make the columns arguments, and that is where dplyr's convenience bites. It
lets you type a column name as if it were an ordinary object, but inside your own
function the name arrives *inside an argument*, one step removed, and you have to
tell dplyr to look inside.

The examples use `penguins_clean`, built in Block 2 from
`data/raw/penguins_raw.csv` ([Which penguins?](index.qmd#which-penguins)).

{{< include include/_catch-up-day1.qmd >}}

## The problem

A first, reasonable attempt that does not work:

```{r}
#| eval: false
summarise_by_species <- function(data, var) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(var, na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)
}

summarise_by_species(penguins_clean, body_mass_g)
# Error in `dplyr::summarise()`:
# ℹ In argument: `mean = mean(var, na.rm = TRUE)`.
# ℹ In group 1: `species = "Adelie"`.
# Caused by error:
# ! object 'body_mass_g' not found
```

The function received `var = body_mass_g`, and `body_mass_g` is plainly a column
of `penguins_clean`. Yet the error says it cannot be found. Why?

## Two meanings of "variable"

dplyr's own guide to programming (`vignette("programming", package = "dplyr")`)
explains this by splitting the word "variable" in two:

- An **env-variable** is a programming object that lives in your R session or
  in a function. You make one with `<-`, or it arrives as a function argument.
- A **data-variable** is a column that lives inside a data frame.

```{r}
#| eval: false
df <- tibble::tibble(x = 1:3)   # df is an env-variable
df$x                            # x is a data-variable inside it
```

Inside `filter()`, `mutate()`, `summarise()` and friends, dplyr lets you type a
data-variable as if it were an env-variable: `summarise(mean = mean(body_mass_g))`
finds the column. This is **data masking**: the data frame "masks" your session,
so its columns are found first. It is what makes interactive dplyr so pleasant.

The trouble starts with **indirection**: the column name is no longer typed in
the verb, but held in an env-variable, here the argument `var`. dplyr sees the
name `var`, finds no column called `var`, and never discovers that `var` holds
the column name you meant.

Think of the argument as an envelope with a column name written inside. dplyr
reads the label on the envelope (`var`), not what is inside it. You need to
tell it to open the envelope.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why exactly does the error say `body_mass_g`?

dplyr looks for a column called `var`, does not find one, and so falls back to
the function's own objects, where it finds the argument `var`. R evaluates
arguments lazily: only now does it work out what `var` holds, by evaluating the
expression the user typed, `body_mass_g`. It evaluates that in the *calling*
environment, your workspace, not inside the data frame. Your workspace has no
object called `body_mass_g`, hence "object 'body_mass_g' not found". The data
mask was applied to the name `var`, never to the column name the user meant.
:::

## Embracing: `{{ }}`

The **embracing operator** `{{ }}` opens the envelope: it tells dplyr "the user
handed me a column name; use that, not the word `var`".

```{r}
#| eval: false
summarise_by_species <- function(data, var) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(mean = mean({{ var }}, na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)
}

summarise_by_species(penguins_clean, body_mass_g)
# # A tibble: 3 x 2
#   species    mean
#   <chr>     <dbl>
# 1 Adelie    3701.
# 2 Gentoo    5076.
# 3 Chinstrap 3733.
```

Embrace the column every time it appears, and embrace the grouping column too if
it is an argument:

```{r}
#| eval: false
summary_grouped <- function(data, var, group) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean = mean({{ var }}, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd   = sd({{ var }}, na.rm = TRUE),
      .by  = {{ group }}
    )
}

summary_grouped(penguins_clean, body_mass_g, species)
summary_grouped(penguins_clean, body_mass_g, island)
```

Only arguments that name columns are embraced. A threshold, a confidence level
or a file name is an ordinary value: use it as it is.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Under the hood (optional)

`{{ var }}` is shorthand for `!!enquo(var)`. `rlang::enquo()` captures the
argument as a *quosure* (the expression plus the environment it came from), and
`!!` injects it back into the verb. You almost never need to write
`enquo()`/`!!` by hand, but seeing the expansion demystifies the braces: they
capture, then inject.
:::

### Activity 1: fix the broken function

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Activity 1: fix the broken function
::::
::::{.task-container}

Identify the problem and fix it.

```{r}
#| eval: false
my_filter <- function(data, var, threshold) {
  data |> dplyr::filter(var > threshold)
}
my_filter(penguins_clean, body_mass_g, 4000)
# Error in `dplyr::filter()`:
# ℹ In argument: `var > threshold`.
# Caused by error:
# ! object 'body_mass_g' not found
```

::::
:::


`r hide("Solution")`

`filter()` uses data masking, but `var` is not embraced, so dplyr reads the
label on the envelope: it looks for a column called `var`, fails, and falls back
to the argument, which evaluates `body_mass_g` outside the data. Embrace `var`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
my_filter <- function(data, var, threshold) {
  data |> dplyr::filter({{ var }} > threshold)
}
```

`threshold` does not need embracing: it is an ordinary number, not a column
name.


`r unhide()`

## Two kinds of column argument

Column names are used in two different ways in the tidyverse:

| | Data masking | Tidy selection |
|---|---|---|
| **What the column name does** | Stands for the column's *values*, which you compute with | Labels a column you want to *pick* |
| **Typical code** | `filter(body_mass_g > 4000)`, `mutate(kg = body_mass_g / 1000)`, `summarise(m = mean(body_mass_g))`, `arrange(desc(body_mass_g))`, `aes(x = body_mass_g)` | `select(species, body_mass_g)`, `select(starts_with("bill"))`, `pivot_longer(cols = ends_with("_mm"))`, `across(.cols = where(is.numeric))`, `.by = species` |
| **Helpers such as `starts_with()`, `where()`** | No | Yes |

To filter penguins by mass you compute `body_mass_g > 4000` for every row: the
values matter, so it is data masking. To select the mass column you compute
nothing; only the name matters, so it is tidy selection.

**How to tell, without memorising.** Two quick tests:

1. **Read the help page.** In `?filter` or `?select`, each argument is labelled
   `<data-masking>` or `<tidy-select>`.
2. **Ask what you could write there.** If you could write `body_mass_g + 1`, it
   is data masking. If you could write `bill_length_mm:body_mass_g` or
   `starts_with("bill")`, it is tidy selection. (This test comes from *R for Data
   Science*, chapter 25.)

Either way, **a bare column name passed through your function is embraced with
`{{ }}`.** The two kinds differ only when the name arrives as a string, which is
the next section.

### Activity 2: identify the kind

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Activity 2: identify the kind
::::
::::{.task-container}

For each call, choose whether the column reference is data masking, tidy
selection, or both (in different arguments).

1. `filter(penguins_clean, body_mass_g > 4000)` `r mcq(c(answer = "data masking", "tidy selection", "both"))`
2. `select(penguins_clean, species, body_mass_g)` `r mcq(c("data masking", answer = "tidy selection", "both"))`
3. `mutate(penguins_clean, mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000)` `r mcq(c(answer = "data masking", "tidy selection", "both"))`
4. `pivot_longer(penguins_clean, cols = ends_with("_mm"))` `r mcq(c("data masking", answer = "tidy selection", "both"))`
5. `summarise(penguins_clean, mean(body_mass_g), .by = species)` `r mcq(c("data masking", "tidy selection", answer = "both"))`
6. `select(penguins_clean, starts_with("bill"))` `r mcq(c("data masking", answer = "tidy selection", "both"))`
7. `arrange(penguins_clean, desc(body_mass_g))` `r mcq(c(answer = "data masking", "tidy selection", "both"))`
8. `filter_out(penguins_clean, body_mass_g > 4000)` `r mcq(c(answer = "data masking", "tidy selection", "both"))`
9. `summarise(penguins_clean, across(where(is.numeric), mean))` `r mcq(c("data masking", "tidy selection", answer = "both"))`

::::
:::


`r hide("Explanations")`

1. **Data masking.** A comparison is computed for every row.
2. **Tidy selection.** Columns picked by name.
3. **Data masking.** A new value computed from existing values.
4. **Tidy selection** (the `cols` argument).
5. **Both.** `mean(body_mass_g)` is data masking; `.by` is tidy selection (it
   picks the grouping column by name).
6. **Tidy selection.** A helper picks by name pattern.
7. **Data masking.** Sorting by computed values.
8. **Data masking.** A comparison is computed for every row, as in `filter()`.
9. **Both.** `summarise()` is data masking, and `across()` is used inside it,
   but `across()`'s `.cols` argument is tidy selection, so `where()` works there.
   `across()` is the bridge between the two kinds; Activity 4 uses it.


`r unhide()`

## When the name arrives as a string

So far the column name arrived bare, as the user typed it. Often it arrives as
a string instead: from a vector of names you loop over, a configuration file, or
a Shiny input. `{{ }}` is for bare names only. A string needs a different
pattern, and here the two kinds of argument part ways:

- **Data masking:** look the string up with the `.data` pronoun,
  `.data[[var_name]]`.
- **Tidy selection:** wrap the string, or a character vector of strings, in
  `all_of()`.

The commonest reason for strings is a loop over column names, as in Block 4:

```{r}
#| eval: false
for (var in c("bill_length_mm", "flipper_length_mm")) {
  penguins_clean |>
    dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(.data[[var]], na.rm = TRUE), .by = species) |>
    print()
}
# # A tibble: 3 x 2
#   species    mean
#   <chr>     <dbl>
# 1 Adelie     38.8
# 2 Gentoo     47.5
# 3 Chinstrap  48.8
# # A tibble: 3 x 2
#   species    mean
#   <chr>     <dbl>
# 1 Adelie     190.
# 2 Gentoo     217.
# 3 Chinstrap  196.
```

In the envelope picture, `.data[[var]]` says: "this envelope holds a string;
find the column with that name". `.data` is not a data frame you can use
elsewhere: it works only inside data-masking verbs.

The same idea, wrapped in a function:

```{r}
#| eval: false
summarise_by_string <- function(data, var_name) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(.data[[var_name]], na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)
}

summarise_by_string(penguins_clean, "body_mass_g")
```

### Activity 3: fix the warning

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Activity 3: fix the warning
::::
::::{.task-container}

This one runs, but not cleanly. Identify and fix the problem.

```{r}
#| eval: false
keep_columns <- function(data, cols) {
  data |> dplyr::select(cols)
}
keep_columns(penguins_clean, c("species", "body_mass_g"))
# Warning message:
# Using an external vector in selections was deprecated in tidyselect 1.1.0.
# ℹ Please use `all_of()` or `any_of()` instead.
#   # Was:
#   data %>% select(cols)
#
#   # Now:
#   data %>% select(all_of(cols))
```

::::
:::


`r hide("Solution")`

It returns the right two columns, but only because tidyselect guesses that `cols`
is an external character vector of names rather than a column called `cols`. That
guess is ambiguous (if the data ever gained a column named `cols`, it would be
selected instead) and is deprecated, so it warns today and may error in future.
Say what you mean by wrapping the vector in `all_of()`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
keep_columns <- function(data, cols) {
  data |> dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(cols))
}
```

If instead the function takes a *bare* name, embracing works: `select({{ cols }})`.
The right tool depends on how the input arrives: bare (`{{ }}`) or as strings
(`all_of()`).


`r unhide()`

### Activity 4: predict the result

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Activity 4: predict the result
::::
::::{.task-container}

Before running anything, predict what each call does: does it succeed, return
the wrong answer, or error? Then explain why, using the envelope picture.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# (i) embracing a string
summarise_mean <- function(data, var) {
  data |> dplyr::summarise(mean = mean({{ var }}, na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)
}
summarise_mean(penguins_clean, "body_mass_g")

# (ii) a string into a data-masking verb without .data
summarise_mean_str <- function(data, var_name) {
  data |> dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(var_name, na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)
}
summarise_mean_str(penguins_clean, "body_mass_g")
```

::::
:::


`r hide("Solution")`

Both **return the wrong answer, with only a warning**: a column of `NA`.

(i) `{{ }}` opens the envelope and finds the string `"body_mass_g"`, not a
column name. `mean()` then receives a single piece of text, and the mean of a
piece of text is `NA`, with the warning "argument is not numeric or logical:
returning NA". Embracing is for bare names; a string needs `.data[[ ]]`.

(ii) `var_name` is not embraced, so dplyr looks for a column called `var_name`,
fails, and finds the argument, which holds the string `"body_mass_g"`. It
computes the mean of that string: `NA` again. Nothing told dplyr to treat the
string as a column name; that is the job of `.data[[var_name]]`.

The general lesson: passing the wrong *kind* of name to a data-masking verb
rarely errors loudly. It often produces `NA` with at most a warning, which is
more dangerous than an error. Match the pattern to how the name arrives.


`r unhide()`

## The bridge: `across()`

Sometimes you need both kinds in one call: *pick* several columns, then
*compute* with each. `across()` does exactly that. It is used inside a
data-masking verb such as `summarise()` or `mutate()`, and its `.cols` argument
is tidy selection, so `all_of()`, `starts_with()` and `where()` all work there.

### Activity 5: the bridge

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Activity 5: the bridge
::::
::::{.task-container}

Write `mean_of_columns(data, cols)` that takes a character vector of column names
and returns the mean of each, grouped by species.

::::
:::


`r hide("Solution")`

```{r}
#| eval: false
mean_of_columns <- function(data, cols) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(cols), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      .by = species
    )
}

mean_of_columns(penguins_clean, c("body_mass_g", "flipper_length_mm"))
# # A tibble: 3 x 3
#   species   body_mass_g flipper_length_mm
#   <chr>           <dbl>             <dbl>
# 1 Adelie          3701.              190.
# 2 Gentoo          5076.              217.
# 3 Chinstrap       3733.              196.
```

The strings arrive in `.cols`, a tidy-selection argument, so they are wrapped in
`all_of()`. The function `\(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)` is then applied to each
selected column. If the user should pass bare names or helpers instead, embrace
the argument: `across({{ cols }}, ...)` accepts `c(body_mass_g, bill_length_mm)`
or `ends_with("_mm")`.


`r unhide()`

## Naming the output columns

For *output* column names built from an argument, `=` is not enough: with `=`
the name is used literally, so `"{{ var }}_mean" = …` makes a column called
`{{ var }}_mean`. The **walrus operator** `:=` lets rlang fill in `{{ var }}`,
using glue-style name injection:

```{r}
#| eval: false
summarise_dynamic <- function(data, var) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      "{{ var }}_mean" := mean({{ var }}, na.rm = TRUE),
      "{{ var }}_sd"   := sd({{ var }}, na.rm = TRUE),
      .by = species
    )
}

summarise_dynamic(penguins_clean, body_mass_g)
# # A tibble: 3 x 3
#   species   body_mass_g_mean body_mass_g_sd
#   <chr>                <dbl>          <dbl>
# 1 Adelie               3701.           459.
# 2 Gentoo               5076.           504.
# 3 Chinstrap            3733.           384.
```

Two things happen on the left of `:=`. `"{{ var }}_mean"` is glue-style injection,
replacing `{{ var }}` with the argument's name; `:=` is the assignment that lets
rlang do that injection (with `=` the name is used literally). Both are needed.
If the name is held in a string instead, use single braces: `"{var_name}_mean" :=`.

The same trick works for text that is not a column name, such as a plot title or
axis label: `rlang::englue("Mean of {{ var }}")` returns the string
`"Mean of body_mass_g"`. The payoff uses it.

## Choosing the pattern

The patterns above each answer one combination of two questions:

1. **How does the column name arrive?** Bare, as the user typed it; or as a
   string or character vector?
2. **What kind of argument receives it?** Data masking or tidy selection (check
   the help page)?

| The name arrives as… | …into data masking | …into tidy selection |
|---|---|---|
| A bare name | `{{ var }}` | `{{ var }}` |
| A string | `.data[[var]]` | `all_of(var)` |
| A character vector | `across(all_of(vars), f)` | `all_of(vars)` |

And for new **output** names: `"{{ var }}_mean" :=` (bare) or
`"{var_name}_mean" :=` (string). Memorise the first row; the rest is reference.

### Activity 6: choose the pattern

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Activity 6: choose the pattern
::::
::::{.task-container}

For each scenario, name the correct pattern from the table, then write the
function. (a), (b) and (d) group by `species`.

(a) `var` arrives as a **bare name**; compute its mean (data masking).

(b) `var_name` arrives as a **string**; compute its mean (data masking).

(c) `cols` arrives as a **character vector**; select those columns (tidy selection).

(d) `var` arrives as a **bare name**; compute its mean into an output column named
    `<var>_mean` (data masking with a new output name).

::::
:::


`r hide("Solution")`

```{r}
#| eval: false
# (a) bare name, data masking -> {{ }}
summarise_mean <- function(data, var) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(mean = mean({{ var }}, na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)
}

# (b) string, data masking -> .data[[ ]]
summarise_mean_str <- function(data, var_name) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(.data[[var_name]], na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)
}

# (c) character vector, tidy selection -> all_of()
select_cols <- function(data, cols) {
  data |>
    dplyr::select(species, dplyr::all_of(cols))
}

# (d) bare name, new output name -> {{ }} with :=
summarise_named <- function(data, var) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise("{{ var }}_mean" := mean({{ var }}, na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)
}
```

The decision procedure: first ask whether the name arrives bare or as a string;
a bare name is always `{{ }}`. For a string or vector, ask what kind of argument
receives it: data masking (`.data[[ ]]`) or tidy selection (`all_of()`).


`r unhide()`

## The payoff: generalising the pipeline

Until now this block has practised on small, stand-alone functions. Now go back
to the analysis you have been improving all day. Blocks 3 and 4 left two
functions that hardcode the same pair of columns: `make_scatter_plot()` in
`R/functions/plotting_functions.R`, and `fit_model()` in
`R/functions/modelling_functions.R`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
make_scatter_plot <- function(data, sp) {
  data |>
    dplyr::filter(species == sp) |>
    ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
    ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    ggplot2::labs(title = sp, x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)") +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal()
}

fit_model <- function(data) {
  lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = data)
}
```

You generalise both, so that each works for any pair of columns:

- **Activity 7, the plot.** `aes()` uses data masking, so this is the main pattern
  of the block, `{{ }}`, plus `englue()` from *Naming the output columns* for the
  axis labels.
- **Activity 8, the model.** `lm()` is not a tidyverse function, so `{{ }}` does
  not work there. This activity shows what to do instead, and when to take
  column names as strings.

In both, the new arguments default to the columns the functions use now. Existing
calls, including the Block 4 pipeline, keep working unchanged, and the
characterisation test at the end of this section checks that they do. Edit each
function in its file, then `source()` the file again.

### Activity 7: generalise the plot

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Activity 7: generalise the plot
::::
::::{.task-container}

Give `make_scatter_plot()` two new arguments, `x` and `y`, that take bare column
names. Default them to `flipper_length_mm` and `body_mass_g`, so existing calls
still work. Label the axes with the column names. Then plot bill depth against
bill length for Gentoo penguins.

Hint: `aes()` uses data masking.

::::
:::


`r hide("Solution")`

```{r}
#| eval: false
make_scatter_plot <- function(data, sp,
                              x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g) {
  data |>
    dplyr::filter(species == sp) |>
    ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes({{ x }}, {{ y }})) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
    ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    ggplot2::labs(
      title = sp,
      x = rlang::englue("{{ x }}"),
      y = rlang::englue("{{ y }}")
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal()
}

make_scatter_plot(penguins_clean, "Adelie")                                 # as before
make_scatter_plot(penguins_clean, "Gentoo", bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)  # new
```

`aes()` uses data masking, so `x` and `y` are embraced, exactly as in
`summarise()`. `englue()` turns the same arguments into text for the axis labels.
Note that `sp` is *not* embraced: it is an ordinary value (`"Adelie"`) compared
with the `species` column, not a column name.


`r unhide()`

### Activity 8: generalise the model

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Activity 8: generalise the model
::::
::::{.task-container}

Now let `fit_model()` fit any response on any predictor, defaulting to body mass
on flipper length. First, predict: does this work?

```{r}
#| eval: false
fit_model <- function(data,
                      response  = body_mass_g,
                      predictor = flipper_length_mm) {
  lm({{ response }} ~ {{ predictor }}, data = data)
}
```

Then find a version that does work. Hint: `lm()` is base R, not the tidyverse.
How does base R already let you pass column names to `lm()` without evaluating
them?

::::
:::


`r hide("Solution")`

It does **not** work:

```{r}
#| eval: false
fit_model(penguins_clean)
# Error in eval(mf, parent.frame()) : object 'body_mass_g' not found
```

`{{ }}` is understood only by functions that use tidy evaluation: dplyr, tidyr
and ggplot2's `aes()`. `lm()` is not one of them, so to it `{{ response }}` is
just `response` wrapped in two pairs of braces, and the column name is never
found.

Base R already has its own way to pass column names without evaluating them:
the **formula**. So the simplest generalisation takes a formula:

```{r}
#| eval: false
fit_model <- function(data, formula = body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm) {
  lm(formula, data = data)
}

fit_model(penguins_clean)                                 # as before
fit_model(penguins_clean, bill_length_mm ~ bill_depth_mm) # new
```

No tidy evaluation at all. The lesson: before reaching for `{{ }}`, check whether
the function you are calling is a tidyverse function. If it is not, it usually
has its own way of taking column names.

**When the names come from a vector.** To fit the same model to several
responses, as you iterated in Block 4, take the names as strings and build the
formula with base R's `reformulate()`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
fit_model <- function(data,
                      response  = "body_mass_g",
                      predictor = "flipper_length_mm") {
  lm(reformulate(predictor, response = response), data = data)
}

c("body_mass_g", "bill_length_mm") |>
  purrr::set_names() |>
  purrr::map(\(r) fit_model(penguins_clean, r)) |>
  purrr::map(broom::tidy) |>
  purrr::list_rbind(names_to = "response")
# # A tibble: 4 x 6
#   response       term               estimate std.error statistic   p.value
#   <chr>          <chr>                 <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
# 1 body_mass_g    (Intercept)       -5781.     306.        -18.9  5.59e- 55
# 2 body_mass_g    flipper_length_mm    49.7      1.52       32.7  4.37e-107
# 3 bill_length_mm (Intercept)          -7.26     3.20       -2.27 2.38e-  2
# 4 bill_length_mm flipper_length_mm     0.255    0.0159     16.0  1.74e- 43
```

`predictor` can also be a vector, such as
`c("flipper_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm")`, for a model with two predictors.
Strings are the right choice whenever the names come from a vector, a loop or a
file: the same reason you met `.data[[ ]]` and `all_of()`.


`r unhide()`

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Optional: bare names for `lm()`

If you want `fit_model(penguins_clean, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)` with bare
names, you must inject the names into the call yourself, with rlang:

```{r}
#| eval: false
fit_model <- function(data,
                      response  = body_mass_g,
                      predictor = flipper_length_mm) {
  rlang::inject(
    lm(!!rlang::ensym(response) ~ !!rlang::ensym(predictor), data = data)
  )
}
```

`rlang::ensym()` captures the bare name the user typed, and `!!` inside
`rlang::inject()` places it into the formula before `lm()` sees it. This works,
but it is the kind of rlang machinery that most code never needs; the formula
and string versions above are simpler to read and to test.
:::

When you change a function's interface, pin the old behaviour down first with a
**characterisation test**, then confirm the change preserves it. Both versions of
`fit_model()` above pass this test with their defaults:

```{r}
#| eval: false
test_that("fit_model defaults reproduce previous behaviour", {
  m_old <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm,
              data = test_data |> dplyr::filter(species == "Adelie"))
  m_new <- fit_model(test_data |> dplyr::filter(species == "Adelie"))
  expect_equal(coef(m_old), coef(m_new))
})
```

:::{.callout-note}
## The four patterns, on one card

| How the column name arrives | Into data masking | Into tidy selection |
|---|---|---|
| Bare name | `{{ var }}` | `{{ var }}` |
| String | `.data[[var]]` | `all_of(var)` |
| Character vector | `across(all_of(vars), f)` | `all_of(vars)` |
| New output name | `"{{ var }}_mean" :=` or `"{var_name}_mean" :=` | — |

- **Which kind of argument?** Check the help page for `<data-masking>` or
  `<tidy-select>`; or ask whether you could write `x + 1` there (data masking)
  or `starts_with("x")` (tidy selection).
- **Not a tidyverse function?** `{{ }}` does nothing there. Look for its own
  way of taking column names, such as a formula for `lm()`.

rlang has more machinery (`enquo()`, `!!`, `enquos()`, `!!!`), but most code
never needs it.
:::

:::{.callout-note}
**Where this leaves us.** The analysis that began Block 3 as three copy-pasted
blocks is now a set of small, tested functions, applied to every group by one
pipeline, with no hardcoded columns: `make_scatter_plot()` and `fit_model()` take
whichever columns you name. Day 2 asks whether someone else could rerun it:
reproducibility and code review.
:::

## Further reading

- dplyr's vignette *Programming with dplyr*: `vignette("programming", package =
  "dplyr")`. The source of the env-variable and data-variable idea.
- *R for Data Science*, 2nd edition, by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and
  Garrett Grolemund, chapter 25, *Functions*:
  <https://r4ds.hadley.nz/functions.html>. Many short examples of data-frame
  and plot functions.
- rlang's help topics on data masking: `help("topic-data-mask", package =
  "rlang")` and `help("topic-data-mask-programming", package = "rlang")`, which
  groups the patterns into forwarding, names, bridge and transformation
  patterns.
- The metaprogramming chapters of *Advanced R* [@advanced-r], for the theory
  behind quosures and injection.
